topics.name: Inventory: valuation and control
topics.why: The biggest topic on Moodle. FIFO/LIFO/WA and the stock-level formulas are pure method, so drill the numbers.
topics.notes:
Why hold inventory: meet expected demand, buffer between processes, cover future shortages, bulk discounts, seasonal swings, smooth production, maturing (cheese, alcohol), hedge against inflation.

Three types: raw materials, work in progress, finished goods. Holding costs: rent, security, insurance, light, staff, shelving, transport, refrigeration, interest on capital tied up, obsolescence, deterioration. Stockout costs: lost contribution, lost future sales, lost goodwill, production stoppages, labour frustration, urgent small orders.

Re-order level = Max usage × Max lead time Minimum level = ROL − (Normal usage × Normal lead time) Maximum level = ROL − (Min usage × Min lead time) + Re-order quantity Average inventory = Minimum level + ½ × Re-order quantity EOQ = √(2 × Co × D ÷ Ch) Co = cost per order · D = annual demand · Ch = holding cost per unit

Normal lead time = the average of the min and max (11–15 days → 13). Worked (Q1, Part SF525): ROL 6,300 · min 6,300 − 350 × 13 = 1,750 · max 6,300 − 180 × 11 + 6,500 = 10,820.

Minimum level warns management that stock is dangerously low. Maximum level warns that stock is reaching a wasteful level.

FIFO: issues come from the oldest stock, so closing stock is valued at the most recent prices. LIFO: issues come from the newest stock, so closing stock is at the oldest prices. Weighted average: recalculate the average cost after each receipt (total value ÷ total units) and issue at that.

When prices are risingFIFOLIFOWeighted avg
Closing stock valueHighestLowestMiddle
Cost of salesLowestHighestMiddle
Gross profitHighestLowestMiddle

JIT (Japanese philosophy): hold no inventory, suppliers deliver exactly when needed, aim for zero defects. Needs a few reliable suppliers, frequent small deliveries, quality materials. Benefits: frees cash and space, faster throughput, fewer defects (Dell). Risk: one supply disruption stops production (Toyota's brake-part fire). Hard and expensive to introduce.

topics.name: Labour
topics.why: Overtime, idle time, piecework and turnover all have one right method. Practise until the overhead split is automatic.
topics.notes:
Direct labour is traceable to a product (assembler, toy painter). Indirect labour isn't (supervisor, worker moving parts between products).

Time rate: hours × rate Piece rate: units × rate per unit (quality units only) Overtime: basic hours × rate + overtime hours × rate → direct labour + premium: hrs × rate × 0.5 (time-and-a-half), hrs × rate × 1 (double) → normally production overhead Labour turnover % = leavers replaced ÷ average workforce × 100 Average workforce = (opening + closing) ÷ 2

Overtime premium is direct only if the customer asked for the rush job. Otherwise (inefficiency, another department's delay, general policy) it's an overhead, so overtime products don't look dearer.

Idle time: controllable (machine breakdown, slept in, didn't turn machines on) → production overhead. Uncontrollable (power cut) → direct labour.

Kevin Hennessy: 52 hrs at €10, 7 Sat at time-and-a-half, 5 Sun at double. Basic 400 + overtime 120 + premium 35 + 50 = €605.

Differential piecework: pay higher rates on higher output bands. Samantha: 97 units → 80 × €1 + 10 × €1.20 + 7 × €1.30 = €101.10. Duggan Co. turnover: 46 ÷ ((200 + 196) ÷ 2) × 100 = 23.23%.

A good incentive scheme has clear attainable objectives, simple rules, full acceptance (including unions), is fair to both sides, is well communicated, pays promptly, and rewards only those who made the effort.

topics.name: Overheads and absorption
topics.why: Apportionment bases are memory work. OAR and under/over absorption are calculations.
topics.notes:
An overhead is an indirect cost that can't be traced to a unit. It must still be charged to products so the total cost and selling price are right.

  • Allocation: charge a whole cost to the one cost centre that caused it.
  • Apportionment: share a cost between centres on a fair basis.
  • Reapportionment: move service department costs (stores, maintenance) into production departments.
  • Absorption: charge production overheads to units with an absorption rate.
OverheadBasis of apportionment
Rent, rates, insurance, security, building depreciationFloor area
Supervisors' salaries, PRSI, overtime premium, idle timeNumber of employees
Machine depreciation, machine insuranceMachine value or machine hours
PowerMachine hours / kWh
CanteenNumber of employees
Overhead absorption rate (OAR) = Budgeted overheads ÷ Budgeted activity (labour hrs or machine hrs) Absorbed = Actual activity × OAR Absorbed < Actual overheads → UNDER-absorbed → Dr P&L (expense) Absorbed > Actual overheads → OVER-absorbed → Cr P&L (gain)

X Ltd: OAR €2 per labour hour, actual hours 220,000 → absorbed 440,000. Actual overheads 480,000 → under-absorbed €40,000.

Use labour hours for a labour-intensive department and machine hours for a machine-intensive one.

topics.name: Cost and selling price
topics.why: One build-up layout. Get the order right and read what each % is of.
topics.notes:
Direct materials + Direct labour + Direct expenses = PRIME COST + Production overheads = PRODUCTION COST + Administration overheads + Selling & distribution overheads = TOTAL COST + Profit (mark-up on total cost) = SELLING PRICE

TUS Widget (Q1): materials 3m × €5 = 15 · labour: machine ½ hr × €20 = 10 + man 3 hrs × €12 = 36 · direct expenses 8 → prime cost 69. Production OH 20% of prime = 13.80 → production cost 82.80. Admin 10% of production = 8.28, S&D 12.5% of production = 10.35 → total cost 101.43. Profit 25% = 25.36 → selling price €126.79.

Trap: read what each % is "of": prime cost, production cost, direct labour, materials, or a rate per machine hour. Each question mixes them on purpose.

Production overheads: factory rent, insurance, light and heat, rates, security, supervisors' wages, factory depreciation. Admin: stationery, computers, postage, audit fees, clerical and managers' wages. S&D: sales wages, advertising, commission, discounts, transport, customs.

topics.name: Cost classification
topics.why: Definitions. Flashcards are the fastest way.
topics.notes:
Costs are classified by nature (materials, labour, expenses), behaviour (fixed, variable, semi-variable) and function (production, administration, selling and distribution).

  • Direct costs can be traced to a unit (direct materials, direct labour, direct expenses). Indirect costs can't, so they're overheads.
  • Prime cost = all direct costs. Conversion cost = direct labour + direct expenses + production overheads.
  • Product costs (materials, labour, factory overheads) vs period costs (marketing, admin).
  • Fixed: constant within the relevant range (depreciation, rent). Variable: change with activity (materials). Mixed / semi-variable: both (phone: line rental + calls).
  • Sunk costs are already incurred and unrecoverable, so they're irrelevant to decisions. Opportunity cost is the benefit forgone. Relevant costs are future and differ between options.
  • Cost centre: a location or function costs are collected for (a department). Cost unit: a unit of product or service costed (a widget, a batch).

written.q: Outline the advantages and disadvantages of FIFO, LIFO and weighted average stock valuation.
points: FIFO: logical (matches physical flow), closing stock at up-to-date prices · but cost of sales at old prices, so profit is overstated when prices rise
LIFO: cost of sales at current prices (realistic profit) · but closing stock at out-of-date prices, and not allowed under IAS 2 for financial statements
WA: smooths price changes, easy to justify · but needs recalculating after every receipt, and issue prices aren't actual prices paid
Rising prices: FIFO gives the highest profit and closing stock, LIFO the lowest
Choice affects reported profit, tax and stock values in the SOFP

points: Basic 40 × 5 = 200 · overtime 12 × 5 = 60
Direct labour: (40 − 5 idle) × 5 = 175 + overtime 60 = 235
Production overhead: controllable idle 25 + premium 42.50 = 67.50

written.q: Explain allocation, apportionment, reapportionment and absorption of overheads, and give a suitable basis of apportionment for three overheads.
points: Allocation: whole cost to the one cost centre that caused it
Apportionment: shared fairly between cost centres using a basis
Reapportionment: service department costs moved to production departments
Absorption: charged to units with an OAR (per unit, labour hour or machine hour)
Bases: rent and insurance → floor area · supervisors → number of employees · machine depreciation → machine value
